compare.feature: Feedback on structure, pace and filler words

faq.q: Is the first mock interview really free?
faq.a: Yes. Your first session is free and needs no card.

faq.q: Do I speak or type my answers?
faq.a: Speak. The app turns your voice into text and gives feedback on what you said and how you said it: structure, clarity, pace and filler words.

faq.q: What kinds of interviews can I practise?
faq.a: Behavioural, technical, case-style and general HR rounds, for a range of roles and levels. You choose the role and add your résumé for tailored questions.

faq.q: Will it write my answers for me?
faq.a: It coaches you. It suggests a structure and talking points, and you practise in your own words, so you sound like you on the day.

faq.q: Can I use it during a real interview?
faq.a: No. ShortlistPrep is a preparation and practice tool. It is not designed to help you during a live interview, and using it to mislead an employer is against the Terms of use.

faq.q: Who can see my recordings, résumé and photos?
faq.a: Only you. You choose what to keep and you can delete everything at any time.

posts.title: The STAR method, made simple (with a real example)
posts.summary: A four-step structure for behavioural questions, so your answers stop rambling.
body: Behavioural questions start with 'Tell me about a time when...'. The easiest way to answer them clearly is STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

body.h: Situation: set the scene in one or two sentences

body: Say where you were and what was happening. Keep it short. 'Last spring our launch date moved forward by two weeks.'

body.h: Task: say what you were responsible for

body: 'I was leading the release and had to keep quality high with much less time.'
This is the longest part. Use 'I', not 'we', so the interviewer hears your contribution. 'I split the work into three parts, asked each owner for a daily update, and cut two low-priority features.'

body.h: Result: finish with an outcome, ideally a number

body: 'We shipped on time, and support tickets fell by 20 percent.' Many people forget this step, and it is the one that makes the answer memorable.
Reading a STAR answer is easy. Saying it smoothly under mild pressure is a skill, and it improves fast with a few rounds of practice.

posts.title: How to stop saying 'um' in interviews
posts.summary: Filler words are normal. Here is how to make them less noticeable.
body: Everyone uses filler words. The goal is not zero, it is fewer and calmer.

body.h: Replace the filler with a pause

body: A short silence feels long to you and almost invisible to the listener. When you feel an 'um' coming, breathe in and say nothing for a second.

body.h: Slow down at the start of a sentence

body: Most fillers appear when you start speaking before you know where the sentence is going. Take a beat first.
You cannot fix what you cannot hear. Record a practice answer and count the fillers. The number usually drops quickly once you notice it.

posts.title: Answering 'Tell me about yourself' in under two minutes
posts.summary: A simple present-past-future formula for the question every interviewer asks.
body: It sounds easy and trips up almost everyone. The trick is to treat it as a short pitch, not your life story.
One sentence on your current role and your strongest skill.
Two or three highlights that are relevant to this job, with one result you are proud of.
End with what you want next and why this company fits. It naturally hands the conversation back to the interviewer.
Time yourself. If you run over, cut the oldest, least relevant part first.
